meta.title: Who really said "The meaning of life is to find your gift. The purpose of life is to give it away"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Shakespeare. Quote Investigator and Wikiquote both trace it to psychiatrist David Viscott's 1993 book of meditations — and the popular wording is a reshuffle.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The meaning of life is to find your gift. The purpose of life is to give it away'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare. Quote Investigator and Wikiquote trace the line to David Viscott's 1993 book, where it ran in three parts, not two.

answer.label: Not Shakespeare — reworded from David Viscott
answer.sourceLine: Shakespeare never wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive evidence tying the line to Shakespeare (or to Picasso, the other common credit), and traces the earliest strong match to psychiatrist and radio host David Viscott’s 1993 book Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times: A Book of Meditations. Viscott wrote it in three parts — discover, develop, give away — and the familiar two-clause version is a later, unattributed reshuffle that swaps “meaning” and “purpose” and replaces “discover” with “find.”
answer.confidenceText: Both Quote Investigator and Wikiquote independently place this under Viscott, not Shakespeare.

source.excerpt: The purpose of life is to discover your gift. The work of life is to develop it. The meaning of life is to give your gift away.
trail: 1993 — The earliest strong match. David Viscott’s Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times: A Book of Meditations is published by Contemporary Books, containing the three-part saying. Quote Investigator credits Viscott with originating the adage ↗.

1994–1997 — Simplified restatements begin appearing in the press. Quote Investigator’s chronology records instances in the Seattle Times (January 1994 and January 1995), the Atlantic City Press (May 1995), and a February 1997 Chattanooga Times instance attributed to Viscott ↗.

2006 — The wording we know today surfaces: a March 2006 San Francisco Chronicle instance has the words swapped and “find” in place of “discover” ↗. The same year, a two-part version is credited to Joy Golliver in a book epigraph.

Today — The couplet circulates under Shakespeare’s name with no source attached — as on this Goodreads entry ↗, which cites no book. Wikiquote answers it directly in its Misattributed section ↗: “Not by Shakespeare, but from Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times.”
source.excerptNote: This is the three-part original as documented by Quote Investigator and reproduced in collections of Viscott’s quotations. The circulating version keeps the first and last beats, drops the middle one, swaps “meaning” and “purpose,” and changes “discover” to “find.”
source.rightsHolder: The estate of David Viscott and his publisher, Contemporary Books (now part of McGraw-Hill)
source.rightsNote: Rights here have nothing to do with Shakespeare, whose works are long in the public domain — this line simply is not his. The saying was first published in David Viscott’s Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times in 1993, well after the 1931 threshold, so the text remains in copyright and is not free to reproduce at length. The short two-clause version in circulation is an anonymous rewording of that copyrighted sentence, which gives it no independent public-domain status; brief quotation with attribution to Viscott is the safe course.

author.name: David Viscott
author.heading: The man who actually wrote it
author.bio: David Viscott was a Boston-trained psychiatrist who moved to Los Angeles in 1979 as a UCLA psychiatry professor and became one of the first people to practice psychiatry on talk radio, beginning at KABC in 1980. He wrote The Making of a Psychiatrist, The Language of Feelings and Emotionally Free, and hosted the syndicated TV show Getting in Touch with Dr. David Viscott. His 1993 meditation collection Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times contains the line that the internet now hands to Shakespeare.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a modern self-help line with a modern author, so every famous name attached to it is an invention. Quote Investigator addresses the two biggest ones directly.

items.why: Quote Investigator states it has found no substantive evidence ↗ linking the expression to Shakespeare, and Wikiquote files this exact wording under its Misattributed section ↗, naming Viscott's 1993 book as the real source. Shakespeare died in 1616; the line postdates him by roughly 377 years.
The other common credit, especially on Facebook and Pinterest. Quote Investigator reports no substantive evidence ↗ tying the saying to Picasso either.
Quote Investigator notes that a simplified two-part version was credited to Joy Golliver ↗, an author and lecturer on community service, in a 2006 book epigraph — thirteen years after Viscott's book.

items.who: Nobody — it is an anonymous edit
items.why: Even crediting Viscott, the popular two-clause form is not his sentence. His original has three parts and uses “discover”; Quote Investigator's chronology shows the swapped, “find”-based wording appearing by March 2006 ↗. No individual is documented as making the change.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is David Viscott’s, published in 1993; the two-clause wording everyone shares is an anonymous later edit of it — and no part of it is Shakespeare’s ↗.

context.heading: Why it drifted to Shakespeare
lead: The line has the two things a quote needs to go viral without a source: it is short, and it is kind. It offers a whole theory of a life in two clauses, and it asks nothing of the reader except to feel understood. Viscott, a working psychiatrist writing a book of daily meditations, built it as a three-beat sequence with a middle step that does the unglamorous work — develop it. That middle beat is the part the internet dropped.

What survived is a tidier, more quotable couplet with no author attached, and an unattached couplet drifts upward toward the most famous name available. Shakespeare is the default landing site for any English sentence that sounds wise and has lost its paperwork; Picasso plays the same role for anything about art or gifts. Neither man is credited by any source that predates Viscott.
detailsBody: Viscott’s 1993 original runs in three parts: the purpose of life is to discover your gift, the work of life is to develop it, the meaning of life is to give your gift away.

In the popular version, the middle clause is gone, “meaning” and “purpose” have traded places, and “discover” has become “find.” Quote Investigator’s chronology shows simplified two-part restatements circulating in newspapers from January 1994 onward, with a March 2006 San Francisco Chronicle instance showing the words swapped and “find” in place of “discover.”
context.pull: The middle step — the work of life is to develop it — is the part the internet deleted.
